## What brewing actually does

Brewing is dissolving plant solids into water—like a tea bag sitting in a mug. Warmer water speeds that process. Different compounds come out at different speeds, and that is where everyday choices start to matter. Classic infusion studies treated tea steeping as a measurable solid–liquid extraction problem: how fast caffeine and theaflavins leave the leaf, and how the water temperature changes those rates [^1][^2].

**Caffeine** dissolves readily and comes out relatively easily. **L-theanine** is very soluble even at lower temperatures and also comes out early. **EGCG** needs more heat and time. It is also less stable in more alkaline water [^3][^4].

Cold brew is *slower*, not "caffeine-free." Given enough time, cold water can still pull a lot of caffeine.

If you dunk a tea bag for ten seconds, the drink is pale and mild. If you leave it for minutes in hot water, it gets stronger. That is extraction: more time and heat usually mean more compounds in the water—until taste turns too bitter for you.

The snapshot below is an order-of-magnitude guide from the packs and the papers they cite—not a cooking recipe.

| Compound | How it behaves in water | Notes from sources |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Caffeine | Dissolves readily; much more soluble as water heats | About 20 g/L at 20°C; much higher near boiling [^1] |
| L-Theanine | Very soluble even at lower temperatures | About 350 g/L at 25°C; cup yields depend on tea type and brew time [^3] |
| EGCG | Needs more heat; less stable if the brew is too alkaline | Water extraction of green-tea catechins is often most efficient near about 80°C for a timed steep; very hot, long steeps risk degradation [^4] |

Keenan and colleagues measured how much L-theanine actually lands in a real cup. For a 200 mL cup steeped two minutes, they reported roughly **24 mg** in ordinary black tea, lower averages for some specialty blacks and whites, and roughly **8 mg** in the green teas they tested—with brew time as the big dial [^3]. Shaded Japanese greens (Gyokuro, Matcha) can sit higher still; the [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd) keeps those everyday ranges in one place.

Perva-Uzunalić and colleagues mapped how temperature and time change catechin and caffeine recovery from green tea. Short, hot extractions can be efficient; pushing temperature and time too far starts to destroy the very catechins you hoped to pull [^4]. That is the kitchen trade-off in a sentence: hotter and longer can raise EGCG—and bitterness—until the cup tastes like regret.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: extraction rates, cold brew, and the 80°C EGCG trade-off"}
Classic infusion studies treated steeping as solid–liquid extraction: how fast caffeine and theaflavins leave the leaf, and how water temperature changes those rates.[^1][^2] Caffeine dissolves readily—on the order of **20 g/L** at 20°C and much higher near boiling in the pack/Spiro framing.[^1] L-theanine is extremely water-soluble even when cool (about **350 g/L** at 25°C in solubility notes the packs cite), which is why it appears early in a steep.[^3] EGCG needs more heat and time, and it is less stable if the brew turns too alkaline.[^4]

Keenan's group measured real cups: for **200 mL** steeped **two minutes**, ordinary black tea often landed near **24 mg** L-theanine, with lower averages for some specialty blacks/whites and roughly **8 mg** in the greens they tested—brew time was the big dial.[^3] Shaded Japanese greens (Gyokuro, Matcha) can sit higher; see the [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd).

**Cold brew.** Cold water *slows* extraction; it does not delete caffeine. Given enough time (often **12–24 hours** in the literature discussed in the packs), caffeine can reach levels similar to—or above—a short hot steep.[^1]

**Temperature and what you feel later.** Brewing green tea well below **80°C** tends to lower the EGCG-to-caffeine ratio, so the cup you later feel is chemically skewed—not only milder in taste.[^4]
:::

If you want more of the "green tea catechin" side of the cup, hotter water and a bit more time help EGCG extract—but they can also pull more bitter material. Caffeine and L-theanine are already relatively easy to extract.

And here is the cold-brew story people tell: "Cold brew means no caffeine." Cold water only *slows* extraction. Given enough time (often 12–24 hours in the literature discussed in the packs), caffeine in cold brew can reach levels similar to—or even above—a short hot steep.

There is also a quiet bridge from this kitchen scene to Chapter 2: EGCG needs more heat to extract well. Brewing green tea well below **80°C** tends to lower the EGCG-to-caffeine ratio. So temperature is not only about taste—it changes which compounds dominate the cup you later feel.

The leaf has given up its guests. Time to name the three who matter most in everyday talk.

[^3]: Keenan, E. K., et al. (2011). How much theanine in a cup of tea? Effects of tea type and method of preparation. *Food Chemistry, 125*(2), 588–594. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodchem.2010.08.071

[^4]: Perva-Uzunalić, A., et al. (2006). Extraction of active ingredients from green tea (*Camellia sinensis*): Extraction efficiency of major catechins and caffeine. *Food Chemistry, 96*(4), 597–605. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodchem.2005.03.015
